def: A nonlinear function applied after a linear layer, such as ReLU, GELU or sigmoid. Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear map.
Choosing which unlabelled examples to label next, usually the ones the model is least certain about.
An optimizer that keeps running averages of the gradient and its square to give each parameter its own step size. AdamW adds decoupled weight decay.
An input changed by a small, deliberately chosen perturbation that makes a model predict wrongly.
An LLM running in a loop that chooses actions, calls tools and reads the results until a task is done.
A collective operation in which every GPU ends up with the sum (or mean) of a tensor across all GPUs; used to average gradients.
An approximate nearest-neighbour index (such as HNSW or IVF) that finds similar vectors far faster than brute force, at a small cost in recall.
A mechanism that computes each output as a weighted average of values, with weights from query–key similarity: \(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{QK}^\top/\sqrt{d_k})\mathbf V\).
The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative.
Automatic differentiation: the framework records operations and applies the chain rule backwards to get gradients.
Computing gradients of a loss with respect to every parameter by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.
Training models on bootstrap resamples of the data and averaging them to reduce variance; the basis of random forests.
Normalizing each feature using statistics over the mini-batch, then rescaling with learned parameters. Common in CNNs.
\(p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto p(\mathcal D\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\): how to update beliefs with evidence.
A decoding method that keeps the \(b\) most likely partial sequences at every step.
A Transformer encoder pretrained with masked language modelling; used for classification, NER, embeddings and reranking.
Expected error splits into bias², variance and noise. Flexible models lower bias but raise variance.
A keyword ranking function: TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization.
A subword tokenizer built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by virtually stretching dimensions of size 1.
A model is calibrated when its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, e.g. 80% of 0.8 predictions are positive.
Having a model write intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer.
Splitting documents into passages for retrieval. Chunk size and overlap strongly affect RAG quality.
A model that embeds images and text into one space by contrastive training on image–caption pairs; enables zero-shot classification.
A change over time in the relationship between inputs and the target, so a once-good model degrades.
A variable that influences both a treatment and an outcome, creating a spurious association between them.
Learning representations by pulling related pairs together and pushing unrelated ones apart, often with the InfoNCE loss.
Sliding a small learned kernel over an input and computing a weighted sum at each position; the core operation of CNNs.
\(\mathbf x^\top\mathbf y/(\|\mathbf x\|\|\mathbf y\|)\): the cosine of the angle between two vectors.
A model that reads a query and a document together to score relevance; accurate but too slow for first-stage retrieval.
\(H(p,q)=-\sum p\log q\); the standard classification loss and the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model.
Rotating which part of the training data is held out for validation to get a lower-variance estimate of generalization.
A speech-recognition loss that sums over all alignments between audio frames and a shorter output sequence.
Information unavailable at prediction time sneaking into training or validation, inflating offline scores.
A generative model trained to reverse a gradual noising process; generation starts from noise and denoises step by step.
A guarantee that an algorithm's output changes little whether or not any single person's data is included.
Training a small student model to match a larger teacher's soft predictions.
Direct preference optimization: aligning a model on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, without a separate reward model.
Randomly zeroing units during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit; a regularizer.
A nonzero vector \(\mathbf v\) whose direction a matrix preserves: \(\mathbf A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v\).
Evidence lower bound: reconstruction term minus a KL term; the objective maximized by VAEs.
A dense vector representation of a token, item, sentence or image, learned so that similar things are close.
The average loss over the training set; an estimate of the expected loss on the true data distribution.
\(H(p)=-\sum p\log p\): the average surprise of a distribution.
One full pass through the training data.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable's values.
Continuing to train a pretrained model on task-specific data.
An exact attention algorithm that tiles computation in on-chip memory, avoiding the full \(n\times n\) matrix in GPU memory.
Training a velocity field that transports noise to data by regressing on simple interpolation paths.
Sharding weights, gradients and optimizer states across GPUs so each holds only a fraction of the training state.
Generative adversarial network: a generator and discriminator trained against each other.
A distribution over functions; any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian with a kernel covariance.
How well a model performs on data it was not trained on.
\(1-\sum_kp_k^2\): a measure of class mixing used to choose decision-tree splits.
Graph neural network: layers that update each node from messages sent by its neighbours.
The vector of partial derivatives of a function; it points in the direction of steepest increase.
Building an additive model of trees, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss of the current ensemble.
Rescaling gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold to stabilize training.
Repeatedly stepping parameters against the gradient: \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla\mathcal L\).
Several query heads sharing one key–value head, shrinking the KV cache.
Fluent model output that is not supported by facts or sources.
Hierarchical navigable small world graph: a popular ANN index with excellent recall and speed.
Combining keyword (BM25) and dense vector retrieval, often merged with reciprocal rank fusion.
A setting chosen outside training, such as learning rate or tree depth, tuned on validation data.
Learning a policy from expert demonstrations, for example by behaviour cloning.
A contrastive loss: cross-entropy where the matching pair is the correct class among in-batch candidates.
Intersection over union: overlap area divided by combined area of two boxes or masks.
The matrix of first partial derivatives of a vector-valued function.
A recursive estimator that fuses predictions and noisy measurements for linear-Gaussian systems.
Computing dot products in a high-dimensional feature space through a kernel function, without building the features.
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum p\log(p/q)\ge0\): how much \(q\) differs from \(p\). Not symmetric.
Clustering by alternately assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to the mean of their points.
Stored keys and values of previous tokens so each generation step only computes the new token.
Normalizing across the features of each example; standard in Transformers.
The step size of gradient-based optimization; the most important hyperparameter of neural network training.
\(p(\mathcal D\mid\theta)\): how probable the observed data is under given parameters.
Large language model: a large Transformer trained to predict the next token, then usually fine-tuned to follow instructions.
Low-rank adaptation: fine-tuning by learning a low-rank update \(\mathbf{BA}\) beside frozen weights.
An unnormalized score before softmax or sigmoid.
A recurrent network with gates and an additively updated cell state that carries information over long sequences.
Maximum a posteriori: the parameters that maximize likelihood times prior; equivalent to regularized training.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for exposing tools, resources and prompts to AI applications.
An attack that determines whether a specific record was in a model's training data.
A layer that routes each token to a few of many expert networks, growing capacity without growing per-token compute.
Maximum likelihood estimation: choosing parameters that make the observed data most probable.
A document describing a model's intended use, data, evaluation results, limitations and owner.
Estimating expectations or integrals with averages over random samples; error shrinks as \(1/\sqrt N\).
Model predictive control: optimizing a short-horizon plan at each step and applying only the first action.
Running several attention operations in parallel with separate projections and concatenating their outputs.
A classifier that assumes features are independent given the class; a fast baseline for text.
Non-maximum suppression: keeping the highest-scoring box and discarding overlapping duplicates.
\(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf w=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y\): the conditions solved by least-squares regression.
Fitting noise in the training data so that validation performance suffers.
A state estimator that represents the belief with weighted samples and can track multi-modal distributions.
Principal component analysis: projecting data onto the directions of maximum variance (eigenvectors of the covariance).
\(\exp\) of the average negative log-likelihood per token; lower means a better language model.
A feedback controller combining proportional, integral and derivative terms of the error.
Optimizing a policy directly by increasing the log-probability of actions in proportion to their advantage.
Proximal policy optimization: a policy-gradient method that clips the probability ratio to keep updates small.
Of the items predicted positive, the fraction that are truly positive: \(TP/(TP+FP)\).
Instructions planted in input or retrieved content that hijack an LLM application's behaviour.
Storing weights or activations in fewer bits (int8, int4, fp8) to save memory and speed up inference.
Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieving relevant passages and giving them to an LLM to ground its answer.
Of the truly positive items, the fraction the model finds: \(TP/(TP+FN)\).
Any technique that discourages overfitting, such as weight decay, dropout or early stopping.
\(\max(0,z)\): the default activation in many networks; its gradient is 1 for positive inputs.
Writing a random sample as a deterministic function of parameters and independent noise so gradients can flow through it.
A second-stage model that reorders retrieved candidates more accurately, often a cross-encoder.
Adding a block's input to its output, \(\mathbf y=\mathcal F(\mathbf x)+\mathbf x\), which lets very deep networks train.
A model trained on human preference comparisons to score responses; used in RLHF.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: SFT, a reward model trained on preferences, then RL against it with a KL penalty.
Rotary positional embeddings: rotating query and key components by position-dependent angles to encode relative position.
Rapidly-exploring random tree: a sampling-based motion planner that grows a tree toward random samples.
Empirical power laws relating loss to model size, data size and compute.
Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence.
Supervised fine-tuning on curated instruction–response pairs.
Shapley-value attributions that explain a prediction as contributions of each feature.
\(1/(1+e^{-z})\): squashes a score into (0, 1); used for binary probabilities and gates.
\(e^{z_k}/\sum_je^{z_j}\): turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution.
A sequence model built on a linear recurrence that can also be computed as a convolution; efficient for long sequences.
Gradient descent using the gradient of a random mini-batch instead of the full dataset.
Singular value decomposition \(\mathbf A=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^\top\); its truncation gives the best low-rank approximation.
Support vector machine: a classifier that maximizes the margin between classes, made nonlinear with kernels.
Dividing logits by \(T\) before softmax; low values make sampling more deterministic, high values more random.
Splitting individual weight matrices across GPUs so each computes part of every layer.
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: weights words that are frequent in a document but rare overall.
The component that converts text into a sequence of integer token IDs and back.
Sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\).
Reusing a model trained on one task or dataset as the starting point for another.
A neural architecture built from self-attention and feed-forward blocks with residual connections and normalization.
A model too simple to capture the pattern, with high error on both training and validation data.
Variational autoencoder: an encoder–decoder generative model trained by maximizing the ELBO.
Gradients shrinking exponentially as they flow back through many layers or time steps.
\(\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^2]\): the expected squared deviation from the mean.
A system that stores embeddings with metadata and answers nearest-neighbour queries at scale.
A Transformer that treats image patches as tokens.
Vision-language-action model: a vision-language model fine-tuned to output robot actions from images and instructions.
Shrinking weights toward zero each step; the L2 penalty implemented in the optimizer.
An early method that learns word embeddings by predicting context words with negative sampling.
